title: Why Prices Rise Months After a Tariff, Even on Products Made at Home
summary: Explainer built on New York Fed research tracing a tariff from the border to the shelf: importers pay, prices rise slowly, and domestic goods rise too.

assertions.quote: the importing business, the importer of record, pays the duties, not the overseas seller
Paths two and three run through goods made at home, and they share a trait. They're slower.
everyday items began rising a few months after tariffs took effect

verdicts.note: Fed studies of the 2025 tariffs found import prices moved within a month but shelf prices built over several months and input-cost effects took most of a year.

Pass-through arrives with a lag: the direct effect on imports is almost immediate but the domestic channels keep building for the better part of a year as higher input costs move through supply chains, with much of the adjustment at nine to twelve months; pre-tariff inventory is not examined.

Surveyed firms were still adjusting prices more than a year after the tariffs were introduced, which the authors describe as consistent with research showing tariffs pass through to consumer prices incrementally over the better part of a year rather than all at once.

assertions.quote: The tariff applies to the import value, not the shelf price.

verdicts.note: Transport, wholesale and retail margins are roughly half of a typical goods price, so even full pass-through of the duty raises the shelf price by a fraction of the tariff rate.

A 1 percent rise in pre-retail prices raises consumer prices by 0.56 percent; since wholesale, retail and transportation margins are 53 percent of what consumers pay for tradable goods, complete cost pass-through implies a coefficient of about 0.47, which the estimate cannot be distinguished from.

assertions.quote: The collected rate averaged about 2/3 of the announced one, roughly 8 1/2% versus 13.

verdicts.note: Customs revenue divided by import value in 2025 ran well under the headline rates because of USMCA and other exemptions, timing and trade diversion.

The duty rate actually collected ran at roughly two-thirds of the statutory rate throughout, about 8.5 percent against 13 percent at the end of the sample, because of exemptions, exclusions, special entry, drawback and importers shifting away from the most heavily taxed sources.

The average duty rate is below the statutory rate because of exemptions (83 percent of Canadian imports are duty-free under USMCA despite a 35 percent tariff) and because importers shift away from high-tariff goods, with the gap widest in April-May 2025 when imports shifted away from China.
